These efforts are driven by the expanding need for precise modeling of polarization in submillimeter and millimeter wavelengths, a necessity for upcoming astronomical facilities. Our methodology relies on a rigorous, exact, and self-consistent framework for solving Maxwell's equations, which we have implemented in various codes tailored to diverse media. Our initial project involves creating a sophisticated polarization radiative transfer code for the interstellar medium, which will be integrated into the radiative transfer code \textsc{radiative}. Our second project entails developing a polarization radiative transfer code for protoplanetary disks, which will be incorporated into the disk modeling code \textsc{pyradiative}. Finally, our third project is to create a polarization radiative transfer code for exoplanet atmospheres, to be embedded within the atmospheric modeling code \textsc{exoRAD}. In each instance, our approach employs a Monte Carlo method to solve the polarization radiative transfer equation, utilizing established algorithms adapted for polarized radiation. This technique is highly efficient, particularly when dealing with intricate geometries and media structures. Furthermore, we will present preliminary results from these codes, demonstrating their capability to accurately simulate polarization. These tools will facilitate the interpretation of polarized observations from cutting-edge instruments such as ALMA, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Square Kilometre Array. Additionally, we intend to apply these methods to investigate the polarization characteristics of synchrotron radiation from cosmic rays within the interstellar medium. This application is significant for understanding the interstellar magnetic field and its influence on star formation. We will also examine the polarization of synchrotron radiation from cosmic rays in protoplanetary disks, with the goal of determining the magnetic field geometry in these systems. Ultimately, these codes will enable the interpretation of polarized observations from future instruments, thereby advancing our comprehension of the magnetic fields in these critical astronomical environments. However, the dynamic nature of these networks, characterized by frequent user entry and exit, complicates the tracking of influence and public opinion. This paper introduces a method to model the temporal evolution of social and political networks using a time-dependent stochastic process. We demonstrate that the temporal dynamics of a network's state can be represented as a Markov process, where the state is defined by the count of users in distinct roles. Furthermore, we derive a master equation to describe the evolution of the probability distribution for these role counts. By applying this equation to a specific model of social and political networks, we derive an analytical solution for the probability distribution of user roles. This solution enables the calculation of the expected number of users in each role, which is then used to define a user's influence as the product of their role count and the network's total size. Additionally, we derive the probability distribution for the number of users in each role and the joint probability distribution for all user roles. Finally, we apply these analytical results to model the temporal evolution of political networks on Twitter. Our findings indicate that the derived probability distributions align well with empirical data from real-world political networks. We conclude that the proposed method offers a robust framework for modeling the temporal dynamics of social and political networks. This approach facilitates the analysis of network evolution and the monitoring of both user influence and public opinion. Moreover, it can be extended to other types of networks, including biological, ecological, and social systems. Ultimately, this methodology provides a foundation for developing more effective tools to track and analyze the temporal dynamics of various network types. The source code for the numerical simulations is available at: https://github.com/abdullah-ahmed/Temporal-Evolution-of-Social-and-Political-Networks. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the general framework for modeling the temporal evolution of social and political networks; Section 3 details the application of this framework to Twitter political networks; and Section 4 provides concluding remarks. This paper introduces a new method for identifying and correcting such errors by leveraging a novel concept called the "marginalized class." We demonstrate that the probability of a data point belonging to its true class is identical to its probability under its marginalized class; thus, if these two probabilities differ significantly, the point is likely mislabeled. This study examines the ground state wave function for a two-dimensional electron gas within a perpendicular magnetic field, utilizing the exact lowest Landau level (LLL) wave function. We analyze the ground state energy and the structure of the wave function as functions of the filling factor and the ratio of the Coulomb interaction strength to the magnetic length energy. Our findings indicate that the ground state wave function exhibits a distinct structure at the quantum Hall effect plateaus, characterized by a central hole with a radius dependent on the filling factor. Furthermore, we observe that the ground state energy displays a non-trivial structure at the transition between adjacent plateaus. These results align with the concept of a quantum liquid crystal phase at the plateau transition. Additionally, we explore the ground state wave function in a two-dimensional electron gas subjected to a general one-electron potential. We demonstrate that the wave function in this scenario can be expressed as a product of the lowest LLL wave function and a correlation function. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this wave function in describing the ground state of a two-dimensional electron gas. network's topology. While the degree sequence is a fundamental topological feature, it alone cannot fully characterize a graph. This paper introduces a new invariant called the "common neighbor sequence" (CNS), which captures information about the frequency of pairs of nodes sharing $k$ common neighbors for every $k$. We demonstrate that the CNS can be derived from the spectrum of the adjacency matrix and highlight its utility in analyzing graph sequences. Our findings indicate that the CNS governs the asymptotic behavior of these sequences. Furthermore, we show that the degree sequence and CNS are insufficient to determine asymptotic behavior in certain cases, prompting the development of a more refined invariant: the CN sequence. This CN sequence enumerates the number of pairs sharing exactly $k$ common neighbors and fully determines asymptotic behavior. We illustrate the application of these invariants through a case study of Erdős-Rényi random graphs. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential research directions.

**Keywords:** degree sequence, common neighbor sequence, CN sequence, Erdős-Rényi random graph, asymptotic behavior.

DS-NER) has emerged as a promising method for leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled text to enhance NER performance. However, DS-NER relies on the premise that entity mentions within natural language can be generated by combining factual triples. This assumption often fails because natural language mentions are not always simple concatenations of triples; consequently, DS-NER struggles with complex mentions that lack clear references in knowledge bases. To address this, we introduce a new class of entities, termed "non-triple entities," which encompasses all mentions that cannot be formed by merging triples. We propose a novel framework, Knowledge-Graph-Aware NER, designed to identify both triple and non-triple entities. This approach employs a two-stage process: first, it extracts a knowledge graph from the input text, and second, it identifies entities by analyzing the relationships between this graph and the text. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art DS-NER methods. Furthermore, we show that the approach is highly effective at detecting non-triple entities, such as event entities, which are frequently missed by prior DS-NER techniques. This ensemble is characterized by a joint probability distribution for eigenphases that involves a sum of two Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) terms: one dependent on the mean spacing and the other on the spectral form factor. We demonstrate that this distribution can be expressed as a one-dimensional orthogonal ensemble, where the potential $V(x)$ is drawn from GOE and the eigenvalues correspond to the phase shifts of the resulting scattering matrix. Furthermore, we derive a formula for the $S$-number, which quantifies the statistical correlation between eigenphases at distinct energies. This relation is formulated using the moments of the energy distribution of the one-dimensional orthogonal ensemble and can be expanded into a sum of GOE moments. Finally, we establish a connection between the $S$-number and the moments of the distribution of the spectral form factor. These findings offer a novel framework for analyzing spectral statistics in 4-regular quantum graphs and hold potential applications in other contexts. Additionally, we illustrate how the $S$-number can be calculated using the distribution of the spectral form factor's value. These results are validated through numerical simulations of both the one-dimensional orthogonal ensemble and 4-regular quantum graphs. **1. Introduction**

Time series data is prevalent across various domains, including finance, healthcare, and transportation. Traditional time series analysis typically relies on statistical methods, such as ARIMA and VAR, which excel at modeling linear relationships but often fail to represent complex dynamics. Conversely, deep learning models, including RNNs, LSTMs, and GRUs, have demonstrated remarkable success in modeling nonlinear dependencies. However, these models frequently overlook multi-scale characteristics, which are common in real-world data.

This paper proposes a hybrid model designed to capture multi-scale features by combining classical stochastic modeling with deep learning. Specifically, we develop a stochastic model to represent the daily scale and another to model the weekly scale, integrating both into a unified framework. We evaluate the model's performance using financial time series data and demonstrate its applicability to other multi-scale datasets, such as EEG signals and traffic flow records.

**2. Related Work**

**2.1. Stochastic Models**

Financial time series are often modeled using stochastic processes, with the Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) model being a common choice for stock price prediction. However, GBM is limited to a single time scale. To address this, we propose a hybrid model that integrates two stochastic processes to capture both daily and weekly scales.

We demonstrate that these decomposed structures can be generalized to isogenies formed by sequences of kernels with ranks up to $m$, provided that $p > 2m^2$. Furthermore, we outline an application of this decomposition to the computation of $m$-Selmer ranks. This computation is achieved through a variant of the Ladder algorithm, which operates in $O(\log p)$ steps, each requiring only the calculation of a decomposed Richelot isogeny. Consequently, for $p > 2m^2$, the total computational cost corresponds to a single standard Ladder execution. This approach is particularly advantageous for computing $m$-Selmer ranks on supersingular curves over $\mathbb{F}_p$ where $m^2 < p < 2m^2$. In this specific scenario, the algorithm runs in $O(\log m)$ time, significantly outperforming the $O(\log p)$ complexity of the standard Ladder method. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's runtime and memory usage, supported by experimental results. These applications are especially pertinent to the study of isogeny-based cryptography, as they enable the selection of curves with specific $j$-invariants and $m$-torsion structures. This paper introduces a passwordless authentication framework designed for such devices, utilizing a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) to safeguard cryptographic keys and mitigate the risk of physical compromise. Furthermore, we assessed the prototype's performance regarding the overhead introduced by the TEE and the user experience. The results indicate that the solution is well-suited for securing local access to physical devices, though it may introduce a slight delay during the cryptographic operations required for online authentication. Ultimately, we contend that this trade-off is justified, as the solution significantly enhances the user experience by streamlining the authentication process. Our findings indicate that the spectrum of this three-leafed operator exhibits a fractal-like pattern as $\theta$ varies, characterized by a sequence of intervals with gaps that become increasingly sparse. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these operators can be utilized to model the dynamics of quantum walks on graphs. Specifically, we show that the spectrum of the Laplacian with a non-unitary twist corresponds to the spectrum of the Laplacian twisted by $\theta=\pi/2$ combined with a direct sum of two identical copies of the untwisted Laplacian. This equivalence allows us to derive spectral properties for quantum walks on trees. In particular, we prove that the spectrum of a quantum walk on a tree with $n$ leaves, parameterized by $\theta=\pi/2$, is equivalent to the spectrum of a quantum walk on a tree with $n-1$ leaves, for which we have established a complete spectral description. Ultimately, this research highlights the rich spectral properties of Laplacians with non-unitary twists and opens new avenues for investigating their applications in graph theory. This study investigates the phenomenology of dark matter within a strongly-interacting singlet model, which features a singlet scalar coupled to the Standard Model Higgs and a dark $SU(2)$ gauge group. We analyze the model's parameter space using both direct and indirect detection limits alongside constraints from electroweak precision measurements. Our results indicate that a significant portion of the viable parameter space is excluded by indirect detection data. Furthermore, we examine the relic density of the dark matter and examine the implications of the Higgs decay channel $h \to \phi \phi$. Finally, we propose a testable scenario where the dark sector exhibits a dark matter asymmetry. This scenario predicts a dark matter mass of approximately 100 GeV and a small fraction of Higgs decays into two dark fermions, a result that can be verified at the LHC. Additionally, we discuss the potential for detecting dark fermions through missing energy signatures in the $h \to \chi \bar{\chi}$ channel. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for testing the strongly-interacting singlet dark matter model. the number of connected devices is anticipated to surge to 50 billion by 2025. This rapid expansion creates significant challenges for IoT security, as the vast array of devices and the variety of attacks they face make it nearly impossible to secure every device against all threats. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for secure and efficient intrusion detection in IoT environments. This system utilizes a lightweight intrusion detection system (LIDS) deployed on each device, which sends encrypted data to a central cloud-based server. The server processes this data using a federated learning (FL) algorithm to generate a global model that is then distributed back to the devices. This architecture offers two key advantages: first, it enables all devices to benefit from a continuously updated global model that improves detection accuracy over time; and second, it reduces the computational burden on individual devices, as the complex model training is handled by the cloud. **Introduction**

The optimization landscape of deep neural networks is highly non-convex and non-smooth, yet it has been observed that flat-minima optimizers, such as SGD with warmup and a large batch size, frequently outperform well-conditioned alternatives like Adam. This observation is supported by recent studies (e.g., \cite{fineweb2021learning, li2021understanding, li2021effect, li2021flat, li2021flatness, li2021flatness}). In this work, we investigate the underlying reasons for this behavior by analyzing the performance of both flat-minima and well-conditioned optimizers on a simple non-convex, non-smooth loss function. Our results indicate that well-conditioned optimizers tend to converge to a local equilibrium close to a sharp saddle point, while flat-minimum optimizers can escape this equilibrium to find a global optimum. These insights offer a potential explanation for the superior performance of flat-minimum optimizers.

**Related Work**

Previous research has explored the relationship between flatness and generalization in deep learning (e.g., \cite{li2021understanding, li2021flat, li2021flatness, li2021flatness}). However, this paper takes a distinct approach by focusing on the local equilibrium near a saddle point.

\section{Introduction}
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in numerous tasks, including Atari games \citep{mnih2015human}, MuJoCo \citep{Toussaint2012}, and AlphaGo \citep{silver2016mastering}. However, RL remains difficult to deploy in real-world scenarios due to its high sample complexity. Offline RL offers a solution by learning from static datasets, eliminating the need for online interaction with the environment. Despite this, offline RL is inherently more challenging than its online counterpart because the data is often suboptimal, leading to selection bias.

In this work, we introduce a model-based offline RL approach that combines a robust world model with policy gradient updates to learn an optimal policy from offline data. Specifically, we utilize a pre-trained world model to generate additional data, which is then refined by model-based policy gradient updates. Our method is both theoretically grounded and empirically validated, demonstrating superior performance over existing techniques.

Our approach relies on the intrinsic geometric properties of the Newtonian potential. To our knowledge, this specific result has not been previously reported in the literature. Additionally, we provide numerical simulations to illustrate this newly discovered solution. Finally, we outline several open questions for future research. Symmetries Quest. 1 (2016), 1--10, which analyzed the three-body problem under the potential $V(r) = \frac{1}{r} - \frac{\mu}{r^2}$. In this follow-up, we establish that such periodic solutions exist when the bodies start in a scalene configuration, whereas periodicity does not occur if the motion is initiated from an equilateral configuration. These findings are also supported by numerical simulations. Furthermore, we present a generalization of the potential $V(r) = \frac{1}{r} - \frac{\mu}{r^2}$ and derive a corresponding result analogous to the one presented here. This paper introduces a deep learning framework designed to accelerate TCSPC reconstruction. The proposed method employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate the probability distribution of fluorescence lifetimes for each pixel, yielding a more robust and precise output. The CNN architecture is constructed using a series of convolutional and fully connected layers, with the final layer utilizing a soft-max function to generate a probability distribution for the pixel's fluorescence lifetime. This paper introduces a straightforward approach to learning memory for recurrent neural networks that requires no additional parameters or computational overhead. The method involves training a standard recurrent network on a sequence while simultaneously applying a random permutation to the output of each time step. We demonstrate that the network learns to model the original sequence order, effectively creating a network-in-network architecture where the inner layer handles memory and the outer layer performs the primary task. Our experiments show that inverting networks successfully learn to store and retrieve information in a memory-constrained recurrent network, even when the input is noisy. Furthermore, we observe that these networks can acquire long-term dependencies in tasks like the PPM, even when the relevant information appears hundreds of time steps after the target output. Finally, we illustrate that inverting networks can be seamlessly integrated into various architectures, including LSTM and GRU models, to enhance their performance. The technique relies on analyzing the spectral phase of the planet's reflected light, which is derived from the spectral density of intensity fluctuations. We demonstrate that the spectral phase is highly sensitive to the atmospheric scale height, a parameter that varies depending on the dominant atmospheric component. Consequently, this method offers a means to distinguish between atmospheres dominated by nitrogen, oxygen, or carbon dioxide. Additionally, we show that the spectral phase can be extracted from the planet's intensity time series without requiring the simultaneous observation of the host star. Our results indicate that the spectral phase can be measured with a precision of approximately 0.01 radians, enabling the differentiation of atmospheres with scale heights differing by roughly 10%. This level of sensitivity is achievable with a 10-meter class telescope equipped with a high-contrast imaging system, provided the planet is observed for at least 100 minutes. Furthermore, we present a technique for separating the spectral phase of the planet from that of the star, allowing for the measurement of the planet's phase even when the star is not observed concurrently. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future missions, including the Habitable Exoplanet Explorer (HEE) and the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission (HabEx). The HEE mission is expected to achieve a precision of 0.001 radians, while HabEx is projected to reach a precision of 0.0001 radians. Both missions are anticipated to be able to differentiate between atmospheres with scale heights differing by approximately 1%. The results presented here are applicable to any exoplanet with an atmosphere, regardless of its orbital distance from the host star. This includes terrestrial planets, gas giants, and brown dwarfs. Ultimately, this approach provides a means to detect the spectral phase of exoplanets and brown dwarfs even when the host star is not observed simultaneously. While the WIMP hypothesis remains viable, it is not the sole possibility; other candidates include axions, neutrinos, and primordial black holes. This review examines the WIMP scenario, which posits that dark matter consists of particles with masses ranging from keV to TeV. We begin by outlining the theoretical foundations of the WIMP framework, followed by a discussion of the "WIMP miracle," which demonstrates that a WIMP naturally yields the observed dark matter density. Finally, we explore the various experimental methods employed to detect WIMPs. Although the standard WIMP model has not yet been confirmed, it continues to be a primary focus of research. Furthermore, we highlight that the WIMP concept is not entirely isolated from other dark matter theories, as certain connections exist between WIMPs and alternatives such as axions and primordial black holes. These relationships are explored in the concluding section. Overall, this review serves as a comprehensive introduction to the WIMP paradigm and its broader implications within the field of dark matter physics. Additionally, we aim to offer a critical assessment of the current WIMP research landscape, emphasizing the necessity of integrating efforts across both direct and indirect detection methodologies. This approach is essential to maximize the likelihood of uncovering the true nature of dark matter. \section*{1. Introduction}
Domain knowledge has long been acknowledged as a critical component for advancing machine learning research. For instance, in image classification, the presence of a human eye is a vital clue for identifying animals. Similarly, in time series classification, domain expertise is essential for constructing effective models. However, the specific mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning workflows remain poorly understood. This paper aims to clarify these mechanisms and propose a simple yet effective method for integrating domain knowledge into time series classification.

Our approach is straightforward: we identify informative features based on domain expertise and embed them into a neural network as a bias term. This process is intuitive, as the bias term in a neural network functions similarly to domain knowledge by adjusting the decision boundary. We show that injecting a single informative feature as a bias term can achieve significant improvements in time series classification accuracy. Additionally, we discuss how this feature integration can be scaled to handle multiple bias terms. Our results indicate that domain knowledge can be effectively embedded into neural networks, and we contend that future research should investigate more complex integration methods to further enhance performance.

By integrating the method of characteristics with a probabilistic approach, we demonstrate that these solutions are almost surely smooth within a local space-time framework. Furthermore, we derive a precise quantitative estimate for the probability of regularity. These findings offer a novel probabilistic perspective on a established theory regarding regularity and uniqueness. Additionally, we establish a new result concerning the probability of global smoothness. Finally, we provide an illustrative example demonstrating that global smoothness is not guaranteed with probability one. Throughout, we emphasize the interplay between the deterministic and probabilistic components of the model. We also discuss the limitations of our approach, particularly the inability to determine the probability of global smoothness, and outline several open problems for future research. This paper introduces a novel hybrid THz massive MIMO system designed for 6G PSN, utilizing a hybrid analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) architecture that combines both linear and non-linear types. We propose a channel estimation framework based on the orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) algorithm, alongside a maximum likelihood (ML) detector for data processing. Furthermore, we develop a joint design for hybrid digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) and analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) matrices, aiming to minimize mean square error (MSE) while adhering to a total power constraint. To address the non-convexity of the resulting optimization problem, we employ the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to achieve an efficient solution. Finally, numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed hybrid ADC scheme outperforms conventional full-digital and analog schemes, particularly in scenarios involving high-resolution ADCs. Additionally, the proposed hybrid design exhibits superior performance compared to the OMP-based channel estimation and ML-based detection approaches. These findings indicate that the proposed hybrid ADC scheme is a promising solution for THz massive MIMO systems in 6G PSN. In conclusion, this work offers a novel perspective on THz massive MIMO channel estimation and detection, providing valuable insights for the development of 6G PSN. Keywords: 6G, THz communications, hybrid ADC, OMP algorithm, maximum likelihood detector, joint design, power constraint, MSE.

The research is driven by the potential of EV charging to serve as a flexible demand resource for grid operators, thereby reducing the need for costly transmission upgrades. The study is conducted within the context of the European Union's evolving EV charging landscape. The primary objective is to determine the extent to which large-scale EV charging infrastructure can substitute for transmission grid investment. To address this, the work is divided into two main parts. The first section focuses on transmission grid expansion planning, where a novel approach is introduced to model the joint planning of EV charging stations and the transmission grid. This is achieved by developing a new mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the transmission expansion planning problem that incorporates EV charging as a flexible demand resource. The formulation is designed to be scalable for large-scale applications and is validated using the Nordic power system. The findings indicate that integrating EV charging as a flexible demand resource can significantly lower transmission expansion costs. The second section addresses the optimal planning of EV charging stations. A new methodology is proposed to determine the optimal location and size of EV charging stations, considering their impact on the transmission grid. This approach utilizes a two-stage stochastic programming model that accounts for uncertainties in EV charging demand and the transmission network. The proposed method is evaluated through a case study involving a large-scale EV charging network in the Netherlands. The results demonstrate that the optimal placement and sizing of EV charging stations can substantially reduce the required capacity of the transmission grid. Ultimately, this research offers valuable insights for transmission grid operators and EV charging infrastructure providers, enabling them to strategically plan EV charging stations to minimize transmission grid investments. ### 1. Introduction
Recent research indicates that pretraining models on large-scale datasets using self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques yields superior results compared to supervised pretraining (Liu et al., 2021). However, existing methods often demand substantial data augmentation and incur high computational costs. To mitigate these issues, we propose STEM, a simple yet effective approach that trains a single self-supervised model on multiple extrinsic datasets before fine-tuning on the target downstream task. We demonstrate that STEM consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods that utilize multiple extrinsic models during fine-tuning. Additionally, we show that STEM achieves comparable or better performance than methods relying on complex data augmentation and heavy computational overhead.

### 2. Background
**Self-Supervised Learning (SSL):** SSL has achieved remarkable success in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV) by learning representations from unlabeled data. Common techniques include masked language modeling (MLM), contrastive learning, and self-distillation. For instance, BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) utilizes MLM to pretrain on large corpora, while SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020) applies contrastive learning to image data.

**Downstream Task:** A downstream task refers to a specific application trained on a labeled dataset after pretraining. These tasks are prevalent in NLP and CV, such as sentiment analysis, named entity recognition (NER), and machine translation (MT).

(ADMM) algorithm designed to solve the sparse phase retrieval problem, which involves reconstructing a sparse signal from magnitude-only measurements. Our approach is derived by reformulating the original non-convex problem into a convex matrix completion task, for which ADMM provides an efficient solution. We demonstrate that ADMM converges to a global minimizer of the reformulated problem and, consequently, a solution to the original problem. This study investigates the physical mechanisms behind these two peaks by analyzing the interaction between supernova radiation and the circumstellar medium (CSM). We developed a Monte Carlo radiative transfer model to simulate the light curves of hydrogen-poor SLSNe featuring CSM, specifically incorporating the effects of electron scattering and dust absorption. Our results indicate that electron scattering can generate a double peak, but the resulting second peak is significantly brighter than what is observed in SLSNe. Conversely, the dust-absorption model successfully reproduces the double-peak structure seen in these events. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the second peak's brightness is highly sensitive to the CSM's optical depth, allowing for the estimation of the CSM's optical depth ($\tau$) based on the peak's luminosity. By applying this method to the light curves of SLSNe 19cs, SLSNe 19dy, and SLSNe 19fg, we derived $\tau$ values of approximately 0.1, 0.05, and 0.05, respectively. These findings suggest that the CSM in these SLSNe is optically thin, implying that the double-peak phenomenon arises from the interaction between radiation and a thin CSM. Consequently, we conclude that the double-peak feature in these SLSNe is likely caused by the interaction between the supernova and a thin circumstellar shell. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the progenitor systems of SLSNe. These findings suggest that the progenitors of these events are stripped-envelope massive stars that have recently shed their hydrogen envelopes, potentially offering new insights into the formation mechanisms of SLSNe. This study is the first to investigate the influence of tidal effects on the orbital evolution of WD binaries during the CE phase. Future research should explore the impact of these effects on the orbital evolution of WD binaries. Additionally, this work may provide a new perspective on the formation of WD+WD systems. We introduce a distributed algorithm that utilizes the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to solve the associated quadratic program. The algorithm guarantees that the closed-loop system remains robustly stable provided the communication link's capacity exceeds a specific threshold. This threshold is derived by analyzing the small gain theorem alongside the $H_{\infty}$ norm of the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stability margin improves as the network topology approaches a fully connected structure. Finally, we present a numerical example to validate the theoretical findings. Additionally, we show that the stability margin can be enhanced by appropriately selecting the ADMM penalty parameter. This result is significant because it enables the creation of a robust distributed optimal controller for linear systems with bounded inputs, even when the communication channel capacity is limited. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address the stability of distributed optimal control for linear systems with bounded inputs. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 defines the system model and control problem; Section 3 presents the stability analysis and the proposed algorithm; and Section 4 provides a numerical example to illustrate the results. Additionally, we demonstrate that the stability margin can be improved by properly selecting the ADMM penalty parameter.

This note examines an alternative approach to generating neutrino masses by integrating a specific class of string compactifications with the standard seesaw framework. This paper introduces a novel approach to tabular data publishing that achieves differential privacy through a two-stage process. **1. Introduction**

Differential privacy has emerged as a leading framework for protecting privacy in data publishing and data analysis. It ensures that the release of private data does not compromise the privacy of any individual. The Laplace mechanism is a fundamental technique for achieving differential privacy, where noise is added to the output of a query to prevent the disclosure of sensitive information. Consequently, our proposed framework offers a new method for quantifying the uncertainty inherent in cognitive model predictions. Additionally, the framework is applicable to a wide range of cognitive models, including those utilizing neural networks, deep learning, and other computational methods. Ultimately, this research underscores the significance of acknowledging parameter variability in cognitive models and the substantial effect this variability has on the uncertainty of their predictions. By enabling a more robust comparison between models and data, this work advances the field of cognitive modeling and fosters more accurate model assessment. Abstract: Visual analytics (VA) is a rapidly growing field that combines visualization and data analysis to facilitate the exploration and understanding of complex data. This paper reviews the current state of VA, focusing on its applications, challenges, and future directions. We begin by providing an overview of the VA field, including its history, key concepts, and methodologies. We then examine the relationship between VA and other related fields, such as data mining and machine learning. Next, we discuss the various applications of VA, highlighting its benefits and limitations. We also explore the challenges faced by VA researchers and practitioners, such as scalability, interpretability, and user engagement. Finally, we propose a new framework for VA that addresses these challenges and advances the field. This framework is based on the concept of "data-as-artifact," which emphasizes the importance of sharing and reusing data for research and development. We argue that data-as-artifact can improve the reproducibility, transparency, and collaboration of VA research. We illustrate the application of this new approach to VA by providing a case study that demonstrates how data-as-artifact can enhance VA research. We conclude by discussing the potential impact of data-as-artifact on the VA field and its future directions. This study examines the quantum characteristics of such $Z$ solitons, specifically analyzing their energy spectrum and decay channels. We demonstrate that the quantum $Z$ soliton exhibits a decay process mediated by $Z$ decay into $e^+e^-$ pairs, a phenomenon driven by quantum fluctuations within the classical soliton configuration. Furthermore, we find that the $e^+e^-$ pair production rate is highly sensitive to the $e^+e^-$ mass, a factor that can be adjusted by varying the number of fermion generations. This finding suggests that the $e^+e^-$ pair production rate could serve as a potential indicator for the number of fermion generations. Consequently, gravitational wave observations offer a promising avenue for investigating the existence of $Z$ solitons. Furthermore, the study of $Z$ solitons offers a novel framework for exploring the interplay between electroweak symmetry breaking and cosmological phenomena. This research highlights the potential of $Z$ solitons as a bridge connecting particle physics with cosmology. This study employs angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the valence band of the monolayer TMD WSe$_2$. Our findings reveal a complex band structure featuring a global maximum at the K point, a local maximum at the $\Gamma$ point, and a saddle point at the Q point. The sender's objective is to maximize the expected utility for the receiver, defined by the updated belief, minus a penalty term proportional to the entropy of that belief. We demonstrate that this problem is NP-hard and lacks a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a constant factor, unless P=NP. This technique is termed the "multiplicative pressure gradient" (MPG). Results indicate that MPG outperforms other established techniques, such as the standard pressure gradient, the divergence correction method, and the pressure-derivative method. This study examines the sedimentation dynamics of the Lijiang River Reservoir in Guangxi, China, a key facility for flood management, irrigation, and energy production. The study demonstrates that the sedimentation rate increases with rising flow rates, reaching its peak when the river flow rate is 1000 m³/s. This study examines QPPs observed in the hard X-ray emissions of the flare event on April 10, 2012, utilizing data from the RHESSI and STEREO/HoLCEIS instruments. We employed a Bayesian block algorithm to identify QPPs within the hard X-ray light curves and analyzed their temporal and spectral properties. Our findings indicate that the QPPs exhibited a quasi-period of approximately 10 seconds, with the period lengthening as the flare progressed. Furthermore, the amplitude of the hard X-ray light curves increased over time, while the spectral index remained relatively stable. These observations suggest that the QPPs resulted from the periodic injection of non-thermal electrons into the flaring region. We propose that the QPPs were driven by the interaction between the reconnection current sheet and the propagating shock wave. The observed lengthening of the period is attributed to the expansion of the shock wave within the reconnection current sheet. Additionally, the increasing amplitude is likely due to the shock wave's interaction with the reconnection current sheet. This research offers a novel perspective on the generation of QPPs in solar flares and contributes to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying solar eruptions. Ultimately, these findings may assist in predicting solar eruptions and their associated space weather impacts. Mode (TSM) control approach has gained significant traction for its ability to ensure rapid state convergence and high-precision tracking in uncertain nonlinear systems. However, the high-order singularity issue inherent in TSM has hindered its practical application. To address this, the paper introduces a terminal sliding surface (TSS) designed to eliminate this singularity. Furthermore, the study proposes a terminal sliding mode control (TSMC) strategy that leverages the backstepping technique to enhance robustness against model uncertainties. The proposed TSMC features a discontinuous control law that drives the system states toward the TSS in finite time, after which a continuous control law ensures the system reaches the desired equilibrium point in fixed time. The efficacy of the introduced TSMC is validated through simulations involving a robotic manipulator and a synchronous machine. Results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, such as integral terminal sliding mode control and fixed-time sliding mode control, in terms of convergence speed and tracking accuracy. Additionally, the method exhibits strong robustness against parameter variations and external disturbances. Finally, the design procedure for the TSMC is generalized to accommodate a broader class of nonlinear systems. In conclusion, the proposed TSMC achieves fixed-time convergence to the desired equilibrium point and offers superior performance compared to other fixed-time control methods. We demonstrate that if $c_i < 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$, then $S$ admits no non-constant harmonic functions. Furthermore, we establish that $S$ supports no non-constant harmonic functions of polynomial growth, provided at least one sphere has curvature $c_i \leq -1$. These findings extend previous results by Li and Wang, who proved analogous theorems specifically for the case where $n=1$. Additionally, we derive a sufficient condition ensuring that any positive harmonic function on $S$ must be constant. This condition requires that for every $i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, the product of the remaining spheres $S_{j \neq i}$ is non-compact, and the metric on $S_{j \neq i}$ is either of non-positive curvature or a cone metric. The latter definition applies to any Riemannian metric on a manifold with boundary where the interior has non-positive curvature and the boundary is totally geodesic. Consequently, our results apply to any Riemannian metric on $S$ where each spherical factor is either of non-positive curvature or a cone metric. As a specific application, we derive a sufficient condition for the Liouville property for a class of complex manifolds with non-positive bisectional curvature. This class includes the product of compact complex manifolds with Chern curvature bounded above by $-1$ and the product of Stein manifolds with Hessian curvature bounded above by $-1$. In both instances, the metric on the product is defined as the sum of the squares of the metrics on the individual factors. The proof utilizes the maximum principle for the Laplacian on the product of Riemannian manifolds, a technique originally employed by Cheng and Li. We conclude by presenting several open questions regarding the Liouville property on the product of Riemannian manifolds. This work is a joint effort with A. Sakai and Y. Tashiro. This study aims to characterize the evolution of these features by analyzing the temporal dynamics of their intensity fluctuations. We employed the Ca-K 3933.7 Å line from the KPN database, which was processed using the Ca-K Spectral Indexing (KaSI) technique to generate intensity maps. These maps were then analyzed using the Wavelet Transform (WT) method to detect periodicities and evaluate the evolution of intensity variations. Our findings indicate that the AN exhibits a periodicity of approximately 1.5 days, whereas the AR shows a longer periodicity of about 3 days. Consequently, this study offers a new perspective on the evolution of these features, which is essential for comprehending the solar cycle. Additionally, the WT method is applicable to other solar datasets, such as HMI, SDO, and SOHO. Finally, we have developed a Python code to facilitate the analysis of solar data using the WT method. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying a compatible matching within a collection of labeled graphs. We introduce an algorithm that determines existence and, if applicable, constructs such a matching in $O(kn^2)$ time, where $n$ represents the maximum number of vertices among the input graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this problem is NP-complete when the input consists of a single graph labeled with elements from an infinite set. Additionally, we provide a characterization of compatible matchings for a single multi-colored graph, which enables the resolution of the NP-complete scenario in polynomial time relative to the input size. Finally, we examine the problem's connection to the intersection of regular languages. Specifically, we prove that for a single graph, the problem is solvable in polynomial time if the labels are drawn from a finite set, and that the number of states required for a finite automaton recognizing compatible matchings is bounded by a function of the input graphs. Moreover, we establish that this problem is decidable in polynomial time when the input is a single regular language. These findings are derived from the established equivalence between regular languages and labeled graphs. Consequently, we demonstrate that our algorithm for handling finite labels can be adapted to operate in $O(kn^2)$ time for a single regular language, provided the alphabet size is constant. This represents a significant improvement over the previous best-known bound of $O(kn^3)$.

Our primary contribution is a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves a $1-1/e$ approximation ratio, matching the best possible guarantee for the unconstrained case. We also extend these findings to environments with customer heterogeneity, where different customers possess varying valuations for products. In this setting, we propose a polynomial-time algorithm that attains an approximation ratio of $1-1/e-\Omega(1/\sqrt{k})$, where $k$ represents the number of customer types. Furthermore, we show that no polynomial-time algorithm can exceed an approximation ratio of $1-1/e+O(1/\sqrt{k})$. Collectively, these results indicate that the $1-1/e$ barrier is nearly tight for both homogeneous and heterogeneous customer scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate that the problem remains computationally intractable even with only two customer types, proving that a polynomial-time algorithm cannot achieve an approximation ratio better than $1-1/e-1/\sqrt{n}$. Beyond the specific problem, this framework offers a promising avenue for addressing other constrained optimization problems. We conclude by presenting several additional examples of constrained optimization problems that can be solved efficiently using our proposed framework. These findings not only advance the theoretical understanding of assortment optimization but also hold promise for a broader range of applications. This study presents the first comprehensive benchmark of object store performance within a large-scale HPC environment, utilizing the Apache Spark big data framework to simulate realistic workloads. Our findings indicate that while object stores can deliver performance on par with traditional parallel file systems, achieving this requires careful configuration of object store parameters and HPC job settings. The results of this study are anticipated to guide the selection of storage systems for future HPC and big data applications. Specifically, we suggest that object stores are well-suited for workloads characterized by high data locality and a limited number of concurrent users, whereas parallel file systems remain the preferred choice for scenarios involving low data locality and high concurrency. For instance, the pre-processing step benefits from the high I/O throughput of parallel file systems, while the analysis step, which prioritizes data locality, is better served by the object store. This work represents the first systematic evaluation of the performance of HPC workloads on a production-scale object store, and the insights gained are expected to inform future storage system selection decisions. While existing research often attributes this stance to NIMBYists, our analysis of 1,000 U.S. wind project comments reveals that "not in our backyard" is rarely used verbatim. Instead, we propose that the core NIMBYist sentiment stems from a fear of property devaluation. We argue that this fear is often misplaced, as wind turbines can enhance property values by providing renewable energy access. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NIMBYists are statistically more likely to own solar panels, suggesting they might be better positioned to host wind projects themselves. Our findings indicate that the primary driver of NIMBYism is the fear of property value loss, which is frequently exaggerated. Consequently, we propose a solution: allowing landowners to sell a portion of their land to wind project developers. computer science that involves determining if a specific target value can be formed by a subset of given numbers. This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm for solving this problem. The method works by calculating the total count of all possible subset sums and then deducing the presence or absence of particular elements based on the remainder of that count. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach is highly efficient, surpassing existing methods by orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits strong resistance to quantum computing attacks, as it can be transformed into a Grover search problem. Consequently, this work provides a new, efficient solution to the NP-hard subset sum problem. Additionally, the algorithm's high complexity in Grover search space suggests it could serve as a foundation for quantum-resistant encryption schemes. Finally, the paper presents a specific instance of the subset sum problem that is currently unsolvable by quantum computers. This example highlights the problem's quantum resistance and illustrates the potential of the proposed algorithm for quantum-secure cryptography. This study investigates the optical properties of a periodic array of metallic nanowires intended for photovoltaic applications. We demonstrate that the optical characteristics of this array can be precisely controlled by adjusting the wire radius, the spacing between wires, and the dielectric constant of the surrounding medium. Furthermore, we show that the array's behavior can be modeled using a series of concentric metallic cylinders, where the inner cylinders represent the nanowires and the outer cylinders represent the air gaps. This equivalent structure accurately reproduces the optical properties of the original array, thereby confirming the validity of this simplified representation. Finally, we propose that this metallic array can serve as an effective light-trapping layer for thin-film photovoltaic cells. By depositing a thin-film absorber onto the array's surface, the combination achieves higher absorption levels compared to using the thin-film layer in isolation. This enhancement is attributed to the array's ability to capture and confine light within the thin-film region. Consequently, our findings suggest that integrating metallic arrays with thin-film solar cells can significantly improve their light-trapping efficiency. We analyze the holographic dual of a specific class of CFTs featuring a global symmetry group $G$ that decomposes into a direct product $G_1 \times G_2$. In this context, the dual bulk theory is a single AdS space containing two distinct gauge fields, $A_1$ and $A_2$, corresponding to $G_1$ and $G_2$, respectively. We demonstrate that the entanglement entropy of the union of two intervals, where each interval is a fundamental representation of $G_1$ or $G_2$, can be calculated via the area of a minimal surface in AdS/CFT. Furthermore, we show that the entanglement entropy of a single interval, also a fundamental representation of $G_1$ or $G_2$, corresponds to the on-shell action of a point-like particle in AdS/CFT. The second section explores the link between CFT and Quantum Information Theory (QIT). We apply the entanglement entropy of a single interval to investigate entanglement distillation, a fundamental concept in QIT. We prove that the entanglement distillation rate for a single interval in a 1+1 dimensional CFT is governed by the entanglement entropy of that interval. Finally, we extend this analysis to a single interval in a two-dimensional topological order, calculating the entanglement distillation rate using the topological entanglement entropy of the interval. The third section focuses on the entanglement entropy of a single interval in a 1+1 dimensional CFT. We establish that the entanglement entropy of a single interval is equivalent to the logarithm of the partition function of a specific conformal block. Additionally, we derive a formula for the entanglement entropy of a single interval in terms of the conformal blocks of a corresponding block. This derivation enables the calculation of the entanglement entropy for a single interval in a two-dimensional topological order. Collectively, these three sections offer a comprehensive overview of various aspects of Conformal Field Theory. This paper introduces the ICS Cybersecurity Testbed (ICST) standard, designed to ensure interoperability among security solution developers and to facilitate the evaluation of system performance by researchers and vendors. The ICST standard encompasses five key components: the ICS Cybersecurity Testbed Controller (ICTC), the ICS Cybersecurity Testbed Server (ICTS), the ICS Cybersecurity Testbed Database (ICTD), the ICS Cybersecurity Testbed Application (ICTA), and the ICS Cybersecurity Testbed Security System (ICTS). Each component is defined with its specific functions, interfaces, and software requirements. Additionally, the paper outlines the benefits of adhering to this standard and provides guidance on how to achieve compliance. Finally, the ICST standard is compared against existing standards and the NIST testbed framework. The standard is publicly accessible at https://github.com/us-cybercoalition/ICST-Standard. Future research will focus on the standard's implementation, its integration with other frameworks, and the development of a standard-compliant testbed. By establishing this standard, the goal is to enable the creation of a unified testbed ecosystem that promotes the efficient exchange of security solutions and enhances the overall security of industrial control systems. This paper examines the nuanced relationship between stereotypes and pre-trained language models (PLMs). We demonstrate that PLMs inherently encode human-like stereotypes, a phenomenon we term "stereotypicality." Our analysis reveals that these models exhibit a complex interplay of benign, ambivalent, and harmful stereotypicality. Furthermore, we find that these stereotypical representations are not merely artifacts of training data but are also acquired through the models' internal learning processes. To assess the degree of stereotypicality in various contexts, we introduce a new metric called the Stereotypicality Score (ST-Score). Additionally, we develop a novel evaluation benchmark, the Stereotypicality Benchmark (SterBen), to measure the stereotypicality of different scenarios. Our results indicate that the ST-Score effectively captures the nuanced stereotypicality of contexts, and the SterBen offers a robust platform for evaluating PLM stereotypicality. Finally, we explore the implications of the stereotypicality found in PLMs, highlighting the necessity for further research into this area. We introduce a new RET algorithm grounded in a novel concept of 3D beamforming gain, which relies solely on the physical tilt angles of individual antenna elements. This gain is derived from a piecewise linear approximation of a high-fidelity beamforming model. The proposed method is designed to be lightweight, enabling efficient implementation on embedded devices with limited computational resources. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm can be executed using a single processor core, thereby enhancing scalability. Numerical results indicate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to exhaustive search methods while reducing computational complexity by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, the algorithm is versatile and can be integrated into various beamforming optimization frameworks. Finally, we show that the piecewise linear approximation can be extended to model piecewise nonlinear functions, such as power amplifiers, facilitating the optimization of power amplifier tilt. This extension is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving power RET, where the physical tilt angle directly influences the power tilt angle. Numerical evaluations confirm that this extension also delivers significant complexity reductions. In summary, the proposed RET algorithm is versatile, scalable, and delivers superior performance relative to its computational cost. Consequently, it is well-suited for deployment in practical mMIMO systems. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address the piecewise linear approximation of piecewise nonlinear functions in the context of piecewise power modeling for RET. Furthermore, we believe this piecewise approximation methodology can be applied to other piecewise nonlinear functions in wireless communications. Finally, we contend that this research holds significant potential for future studies in wireless communications. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuxuan1994/RET. across various online platforms creates a significant privacy risk, as attackers can easily combine data from multiple sources to reconstruct a detailed profile of an individual. This paper introduces a new privacy-preserving method for user identification that leverages the private similarity structures inherent in user-generated content. Specifically, we employ a private similarity framework to protect the privacy of users on social networks. Our approach enables the secure verification of whether a user from one network is the same individual as a user on another network, all without revealing any underlying similarity structures. We evaluate the proposed method using a real-world dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in safeguarding privacy while maintaining the necessary functionality for user verification. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art privacy-preserving user identification techniques. Furthermore, we illustrate that the privacy protection offered by our approach is comparable to that of the most advanced current solutions. Finally, we confirm that our solution is practical for real-world deployment. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of similarity-based privacy frameworks to user identification. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYuan1995/PPS.

This paper introduces a new FTN signaling method that attains the capacity of an additive white Gaussian noise channel with a rate less than one. The approach utilizes a new class of signal constellations and a detection technique based on the minimum mean square error criterion. We demonstrate that this method can achieve the channel capacity with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of zero, and we provide an analytical expression for the minimum signal-to-noise ratio required to reach the capacity of a single-user FTN channel. Furthermore, we show that the proposed method can surpass the capacity of a Nyquist signaling channel at low SNR values. Finally, we compare our approach with existing FTN signaling methods and find that the proposed method outperforms them in terms of detection reliability. This paper focuses on their representation theory by analyzing their infinite-dimensional analogs of irreducible modules. We define infinite-dimensional analogs of simple modules and establish a necessary condition for their existence. Furthermore, we derive a formula for the character of these modules and demonstrate that their dimension is infinite. Finally, we prove that any simple module of an inverse limit of finite-dimensional irreducible modules corresponds to an irreducible module within the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebra. These findings enable the construction of specific examples of simple modules for this algebra. Additionally, we derive a formula for the dimension of the automorphism group associated with an irreducible module. The study concludes by investigating the character of the inverse limit of finite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebras and its relationship to the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebra.

However, in many practical scenarios, the number of available test subjects is limited, making it difficult to achieve statistical significance. To address this challenge, researchers have developed methods that leverage historical data to enhance the precision of estimating causal effects. This paper introduces a novel approach that utilizes historical data to improve the accuracy of causal effect estimation by applying a Bayesian framework. Leveraging the inherent advantages of HDG, the approach achieves a globally optimal convergence rate of $O(h^k)$, where $k \geq 1$ denotes the polynomial degree used in the HDG discretization. Additionally, an H1-regularity estimate for the time-fractional diffusion equation is established. A key benefit of this method is its ability to decouple the global solution across all interior element interfaces, thereby significantly reducing the number of globally coupled unknowns. Furthermore, the proposed framework is adaptable to other time-fractional partial differential equations. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to validate the theoretical findings. Notably, the HDG method demonstrates superior efficiency compared to standard interior-penalty discontinuous Galerkin (DGP) schemes. Specifically, the HDG method attains the same convergence rate as the DGP method but requires substantially fewer degrees of freedom. For instance, to achieve an accuracy of $10^{-4}$, the HDG method necessitates only 1,000 degrees of freedom, whereas the DGP method requires 1,000,000. This represents a speedup of three orders of magnitude in terms of degrees of freedom. Moreover, the computational cost of HDG is independent of the problem's spatial dimension, whereas the DGP cost scales exponentially with the dimension. Consequently, the HDG method is particularly well-suited for high-dimensional applications. The source code for the proposed HDG method can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYuxuan1994/HDG. However, this strategy introduces a new challenge: the unpredictable nature of cache misses, which can cause significant delays in execution time. This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling the stochastic behavior of cache misses, specifically targeting the prediction of the maximum number of misses within a given time frame. We demonstrate that the distribution of these maximum values adheres to the Gumbel distribution. Leveraging this insight, we develop a new stochastic model for maximum cache misses that integrates the Gumbel distribution with a geometric distribution, resulting in a closed-form mathematical expression. This model is applicable to various cache architectures, including L1, L2, and last-level caches (LLC). Furthermore, we illustrate how the model can be utilized to calculate the probability of experiencing a specific number of cache misses. The proposed methodology is validated using real-world data from the SPEC CPU benchmark suite. Our findings indicate that the model accurately represents the actual distribution of maximum cache misses, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.12%. Additionally, the model successfully predicts the number of maximum cache misses, achieving a MAPE of 1.01%. These results confirm the model's effectiveness and its potential for practical application in real-world scenarios. This study examines the entanglement of a qubit count that far surpasses current experimental capabilities. We demonstrate that a single photon interacting with a crystal can entangle up to 100,000 qubits at once, generating a highly complex entangled state that cannot be described as a collection of pairs entangled with other pairs. Furthermore, we propose a method to verify this state by measuring only a fraction of the qubits. Finally, we analyze the maximal information that can be extracted from such an entangled state, revealing that the information content rises linearly with the number of qubits. This finding suggests that entangling 100,000 qubits would allow for the simultaneous transmission of data from 100,000 distinct sources. These results establish a new frontier in quantum information science, opening the door to the exploration of entanglement across scales previously deemed impossible. The experiment described here is feasible with existing technology and could be conducted in a laboratory setting. The implications of this research are vast, with potential applications ranging from quantum communication to quantum gravity. This study employs *ab initio* molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the reaction dynamics of CO + O2 on a MgO(111) surface. The findings indicate that the reaction proceeds through a two-step mechanism: first, an O-O bond dissociation within the O2 molecule, followed by the reaction of the resulting O atom with CO to yield CO2. This paper introduces a method to demonstrate that other circuit classes, such as those with threshold gates, are also not contained in $FO^-$. The approach involves establishing a connection between $FO^-$ and $AC^0$, where this link is realized by a function computable by a uniform family of polynomial-size circuits with logarithmic depth and constant-size gates. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for $FO^-$ regarding the evaluation of least fixed points, a problem for which no prior lower bound existed. Additionally, we present a novel $FO^-$ lower bound concerning the computation of parity, which is significant because it relies on the assumption $P \neq NP$. Finally, we demonstrate that the $FO^-$ lower bound for computing parity is tight, as it can be achieved using polynomial-size constant-depth circuits. These findings extend to other circuit classes, including $TC^0$, $NC^1$, and $NC^2$. Notably, our proof technique for parity lower bounds in $FO^-$ is applicable to other constant-depth circuit classes, such as $NC^1$, offering a new lower bound for parity in $NC^1$ that improves upon previous results. This distinction highlights the specific power of NOT gates in constant-depth circuits. I. INTRODUCTION Autonomous driving is a rapidly evolving field that has garnered significant attention from both academia and industry. A critical component of autonomous vehicles is the perception system, which gathers information from the environment to support decision-making processes. While various perception techniques exist, such as using LiDAR for object detection, these methods often face limitations, including high costs and susceptibility to environmental conditions. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored fusing data from multiple sources, such as cameras and LiDAR, to enhance perception capabilities. In this work, we propose a new framework for autonomous driving that combines data from both sensors and V2X messages. Our approach leverages the complementary strengths of these data sources to improve overall perception performance. We demonstrate that integrating V2X messages can significantly enhance the detection and localization accuracy of autonomous vehicles. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework can be easily extended to other applications within autonomous driving. The dataset and source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/autodrive-lab/MAAD. The study investigates the oscillation of electron neutrinos into muon neutrinos within the Earth's core, analyzing the oscillation probability under the three-flavor mixing model. Detection is modeled via the inverse beta decay reaction $\bar{\nu}_{e} + p \rightarrow \mu^{-} + n$, with a specific focus on the antineutrino capture of the $^{113}$Cd isotope in Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) detectors. The analysis incorporates the Earth's density profile and magnetic field, alongside the three-flavor neutrino oscillation framework, to determine the probability of flavor change. Results indicate that oscillation probability is influenced by both the neutrino mass and the Earth's magnetic field. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the oscillation probability is highly sensitive to the neutrino mass, with this sensitivity increasing as the mass approaches 0.5 eV. Consequently, this sensitivity can be leveraged to detect non-zero neutrino masses within the 0.1–0.5 eV range. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for future neutrino mass measurements. in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet featuring a ferromagnetic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction has been investigated using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) technique. The study reveals that the ground state phase diagram is highly sensitive to the ratio between the Heisenberg exchange and the DM interaction. Specifically, the tricritical point evolves into a quantum multicritical point, characterized by the coexistence of four distinct phases: a Néel antiferromagnetic (AFM) phase, a canted antiferromagnetic phase, a ferromagnetic phase, and a spin liquid phase. Furthermore, the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction induces a novel phase within the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, termed the "intermediate phase." This phase emerges between the conventional Néel and canted antiferromagnetic states and displays properties akin to a spin liquid. The findings are supported by analyses of the ground state wave function, entanglement entropy, and the scaling behavior of the correlation length. These results offer valuable insights for the design and characterization of quantum materials exhibiting tricritical phenomena. Additionally, the methodology employed holds potential for application to other quantum systems. Finally, the results are compared with experimental data from the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Heisenberg antiferromagnet, Sr$_2$CuOsO$_6$. The observed similarities between the theoretical predictions and experimental observations suggest that Sr$_2$CuOsO$_6$ serves as a promising candidate for realizing quantum multicriticality. Furthermore, the results indicate that Sr$_2$CuOsO$_6$ exhibits an intermediate phase, which may be attributed to the presence of a magnetic impurity. The study also proposes a strategy for identifying such impurities. Ultimately, the results are expected to facilitate the discovery of quantum multicriticality in quantum materials. The paper concludes with a discussion on the broader implications of these findings. Our analysis of the transmission spectrum reveals a significant transit depth of $0.191\pm0.004$ R$_{\odot}/R_{\star}$, indicating a highly inflated planet. This study represents the first transmission spectrum analysis of WASP-127b, offering a promising avenue for future investigations into the atmospheric characteristics of ultra-short period planets. Our findings underscore the necessity of high-resolution spectroscopy for characterizing the atmospheres of small, ultra-short period planets. This approximation is effective for describing the nucleon-nucleon interaction and meson-meson scattering, yielding results that align well with existing data. Furthermore, the methodology is extended to address the nucleon-nucleon interaction by applying a relativistic correction to the nucleon-nucleon spectral function. This correction is formulated as a sum of Gaussians, with parameters determined by fitting the nucleon-nucleon interaction derived from the one-pion exchange mechanism. Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) must maintain a horizontal positioning error of no more than 1 meter with 95% certainty. However, in urban environments, GNSS signals often suffer from blockage and multipath interference, leading to significant inaccuracies. To address this, GNSS data is frequently fused with data from other sensors, such as LiDAR, cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMUs). This paper introduces a robust GNSS/LiDAR fusion framework designed for urban navigation. The proposed system utilizes a robust factor graph (RFKF) to integrate measurements from both sources. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, the framework is highly adaptable and can be easily integrated with other GNSS sensors, such as barometers and GNSS/INS systems. Finally, the framework is also versatile enough to be applied in non-navigation scenarios, such as autonomous driving. We estimate the total mass of the disrupted binary to be approximately $10^{31}$ g, with a separation distance of roughly $10^{11}$ cm. The binary components are likely composed of a mixture of gas and dust. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the double-peak light curve can be effectively modeled using a two-component accretion disk framework. ization, the intergalactic medium (IGM) was highly ionized, with neutral hydrogen fractions ($x_\mathrm{HI}$) dropping below $10^{-4}$ at redshifts $z \gtrsim 5$. Consequently, the IGM's thermal state was primarily governed by the thermalization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). However, the injection of ionizing radiation from the first stars and galaxies, along with the resulting ionization and recombination processes, altered the IGM's thermal evolution. This study examines the thermal history of the IGM from $z=10$ to $z=2$ using a semi-analytic model that incorporates the thermalization of ionizing radiation and the recombination of ions. We find that the IGM temperature is elevated by approximately 10% relative to the standard model, with this excess reaching up to 100 K at $z=6$. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of ionizing radiation on the IGM's thermalization, demonstrating that the thermalization of this radiation is the primary driver of the IGM's thermal evolution. Our results indicate that the thermalization of ionizing radiation is most significant at $z \lesssim 6$, where it accounts for roughly 50% of the total thermal energy in the IGM. Additionally, we investigate the thermalization of ionizing radiation within the context of the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect. We conclude that the tSZ effect is enhanced by approximately 10% due to the thermalization of ionizing radiation. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future observations of the tSZ effect. This research underscores the necessity of accounting for the thermalization of ionizing radiation when analyzing the tSZ effect. This study introduces a coupled DIC-CP-FEM framework designed to determine the crystallographic orientation and elastic properties of face-centered cubic (FCC) polycrystalline materials. The process begins by applying a known deformation to the sample, followed by capturing images of the surface using DIC. These images are then analyzed via a finite element model to simulate the same deformation. A cost function is minimized to identify the most probable initial crystallographic orientations and elastic moduli by comparing DIC-derived strain data with FE-predicted strains. This approach was validated through simulations of a single crystal under uniaxial tension and an experimental investigation of a polycrystalline copper sample. The results demonstrate that the method can accurately estimate crystallographic orientations and elastic properties, even when the sample is subjected to complex, non-uniform deformations. Furthermore, the study confirms that this technique can be applied to real experiments, enabling the characterization of crystallographic orientations and elastic properties in actual materials. This capability is particularly valuable for investigating the anisotropic elastic behavior of materials, which is essential for understanding their plastic deformation mechanisms. Additionally, the method offers a viable alternative for determining crystallographic orientations in materials where such data is unavailable. Finally, the paper discusses the limitations of the proposed method and suggests potential future enhancements. Collectively, this work establishes a foundation for developing a novel, non-destructive technique to characterize the crystallographic orientation and elastic properties of materials.
